lead: Right of way is not a licence. Rules 14 to 17 limit every boat, and above all the right-of-way boat: avoid contact, give room when you gain right of way or change course, and do not luff a boat you caught from astern.

qa.q: Rule 14: if I have right of way, do I still have to avoid a collision?
qa.a: Yes: every boat must **avoid contact if reasonably possible**. A right-of-way boat need not act until it is clear the other is not keeping clear; from then on she must, and a hail is no substitute.

blocks.p: Every boat must **avoid contact with another boat if reasonably possible**, and must not cause contact between other boats or between a boat and an object. A right-of-way boat, or one sailing within room she is entitled to, need not act until it is clear that the other boat is not keeping clear or giving that room. From then on she must, and a hail is no substitute.

fig.note: Port is not keeping clear: now starboard must act too

blocks.p: Only what is reasonably possible is asked: a boat given no time to react, or one that could escape only by hitting a third boat, breaks nothing. Contact by any part of a boat or her equipment counts. Avoiding early is always allowed.

qa.q: After contact with no damage, is the right-of-way boat penalised too?
qa.a: No: she broke **rule 14** but is exonerated under rule 43.1(c). With damage or injury she is penalised too; the keep-clear boat broke her own rule and rule 14 and takes two turns.

blocks.p: The no-damage exoneration is only for a right-of-way boat or one sailing within her room or mark-room. A keep-clear boat that touches takes a Two-Turns Penalty promptly after getting well clear, protest or not. A boat taking a penalty keeps clear of others (rule 21), and a boat no longer racing can still be penalised under rule 14 for injury or serious damage.

qa.q: Rule 15: after I tack onto starboard, must I give the other boat room?
qa.a: Yes, at first: when you **acquire right of way** by your own action, such as tacking or gybing onto starboard, you must initially give the other boat room to keep clear. Not when her own tack gave it to you.

blocks.p: When you **acquire right of way** by your own action, you must initially give the other boat **room to keep clear**: after tacking or gybing onto starboard, tacking close to leeward of her, overlapping her to leeward from clear astern, or getting back to the pre-start side.

tiles.name: Your tack: rule 15
tiles.note: she needs room to keep clear

blocks.p: It does not apply when you gain right of way because of the other boat's actions, such as her tack or gybe, or when you had it all along. "Initially" means just that: once she has had room, her ordinary duty takes over. Room is a prompt, seamanlike manoeuvre, even a sharp bear-away; no rule sets a distance for "tacking too close".

sections.title: Turn only as fast as she can answer

qa.q: Rule 16.1: can the leeward boat luff suddenly into the windward boat?
qa.a: No: a **right-of-way boat that changes course** must give the other boat room to keep clear in a seamanlike way. She may alter as often as she likes, but only as fast as the other can respond.

blocks.p: When a **right-of-way boat changes course**, she must give the other boat room to keep clear. That binds the leeward boat who luffs, the starboard-tack boat who luffs or bears away and the boat clear ahead, before the start as well as after it.

fig.note: You luff slowly: the windward boat has room to respond

blocks.p: Room is judged in the existing conditions: the other boat must be able to respond in a seamanlike way without hitting a third boat or an obstruction. If she has one such way out and misjudges it, the breach is hers. Slowing down on a steady heading is not a change of course. No hail is required, "Hold your course!" binds nobody, and you may alter as often as you like, even below your proper course.
Rule 16.1 limits only the right-of-way boat. A keep-clear boat that sails into her simply fails to keep clear; one robbed of room by a sudden turn is exonerated.

sections.title: No bearing away at a boat ducking you

qa.q: Rule 16.2: can a starboard boat bear away at me while I duck her on a beat?
qa.a: No: on a beat, when a port-tack boat is passing to leeward of her, the **starboard-tack boat must not bear away** if port would then have to change course immediately to keep clear. Holding her course breaks nothing.

blocks.p: On a beat to windward, when a port-tack boat is keeping clear by sailing to pass to leeward of a starboard-tack boat, the **starboard-tack boat must not bear away** if the port-tack boat would then have to change course immediately to go on keeping clear.

fig.note: Starboard bears away at the ducking boat: rule 16.2

blocks.p: The rule is narrow. It applies only on a beat, only to a bear-away (a luff is judged by rule 16.1) and only if the other boat must react at once: five lengths away she need not. A header is no excuse. A starboard-tack boat that holds her course breaks nothing, and a breach costs two turns even without contact.

sections.title: Caught her from astern: no luffing

qa.q: Rule 17: can I luff a boat I overlapped to leeward from behind?
qa.a: Not above your proper course: under **rule 17**, a boat that becomes overlapped to leeward from clear astern within two hull lengths may not sail above it while the boats stay on the same tack and overlapped within that distance.

refs: RRS 17, RRS definition Leeward and Windward

blocks.p: If you become overlapped **to leeward from clear astern within two of your hull lengths**, you may not sail above your proper course while the boats stay on the same tack and overlapped within that distance, unless you promptly pass astern of her.

blocks.p: Rule 17 limits how high you sail and nothing else: you keep right of way and the windward boat still keeps clear. Your proper course is your own and may include luffing round an obstruction, heading for more wind or shooting the finishing line. You may sail below it and come back up to it. A gybe or a broken overlap ends the limit; a new overlap from astern starts it again.
